meta.headline: NEW (2026-06-29) — BOARD DIRECTION (OFFICIAL STANCE): Keepance competes head-on to be the LEADING financial-advisor AI — not a retreat to a niche — and positions as a simple, powerful AI app (connect your files → ask cited questions → living Client Map), NEVER a note-taker. We win on simplicity + AI-first clarity, not integration breadth ('connect 60 things' is the incumbent Jump's failure mode — we won't become it). Jameson went through Jump firsthand: its AI is scattered and hard to use, and it's still a note-taker at its core — that's the opening. This SUPERSEDES the 'reposition away from advisors / retreat to a narrow wedge' recommendation in the 2026-06-28 competitive analysis + strategic advisor memo (kept as competitor/market intel, not direction); see the Strategy tab. ——— STILL IN FORCE — PROOF SPRINT (2026-06-25): go ALL-IN ON FIRST USERS for about two months. Freeze big new features and use the demo to turn a handful of real advisors into weekly users — starting with the design partner (Jameson's wife), then her firm, then peers. Two independent assessments (our own research + an independent Codex review) agree the binding constraint is distribution + trust, not more features. The full Strategic Advisor Memo (06-28) stays on the board as market/competitor intel (see the 'Strategic Memo' tab), and the honest 'where your data goes' trust sheet, demo session plan, and FutureVault read remain on Strategy / Competitive / Sales.

sections.title: Lantern
sections.headline: The foundation is built. We are proving it before the next product push.
sections.lead: Lantern is no longer a blank idea or a small prototype. A large CRM, meeting, search, document, email, workflow, and trust foundation already exists. The job now is to prove that foundation, organize it around one clear advisor experience, and finish the parts that let a firm replace Wealthbox and Jump.

proof.label: of the mapped foundation is proven working
proof.accessible: 54 of 81 mapped foundation items are proven working
proof.caveat: This number measures proof coverage, not time or launch readiness. The remaining 27 items are not all the same size. A product can contain many working parts and still need a reliable installer, safe team permissions, and one complete end-to-end journey.

glance.label: Where we are
glance.title: A strong but uneven foundation
glance.text: Most of the important engines exist. Some are polished, some are partial, and a smaller group still needs proof or repair.

glance.label: Where we are going
glance.title: One calm advisor workspace
glance.text: Today, CRM, Meetings, and Ask should work together well enough that an advisor can replace Wealthbox and Jump.

glance.label: How much is left
glance.title: One proof stage, then three product moves
glance.text: Finish the current control day, fix team access, connect the four main areas, and prove one complete advisor journey before final release checks.

sections.pathIntro: This is the honest progress picture. It shows completed stages and remaining work without inventing a fake overall percentage.

stages.name: 1. Foundation assembled
stages.text: CRM, meetings, cited search, email, documents, tasks, workflows, intake, history, and trust systems exist.

stages.name: 2. Control day
stages.text: Prove that one exact Windows installer can install, visibly open, close, and reopen on all three Windows computers.

stages.name: 3. Product focus
stages.text: Add firm-safe permissions, make the four main areas feel like one product, and preserve the client as the advisor moves through the day.

stages.name: 4. Advisor-ready v1
stages.text: Prove one complete Wealthbox-plus-Jump replacement journey, finish release checks, and put it in front of real advisors.

sections.doorsTitle: The product we are organizing around
sections.doorsIntro: Lantern keeps four main areas. Everything else belongs inside them or in Settings.

doors.name: Today
doors.text: A clear plan for the advisor's day: meetings, priorities, follow-ups, and work that needs attention.

doors.name: CRM
doors.text: Clients, work, calendar, mail, reports, intake, and activity all live here.

doors.name: Meetings
doors.text: Prepare, capture, summarize, review, approve, and create the right follow-up work.

doors.name: Ask
doors.text: Search across the firm, get short answers with sources, and safely propose useful actions.

built: A deep CRM base: clients, tasks, workflows, pipelines, email, intake, documents, reports, activity, and audit history.
A meeting system with preparation, notes, transcripts, summaries, action review, and follow-up foundations.
A cited Ask experience and the local search, privacy, proposal, and receipt systems behind it.
One reviewed save, close, reopen, and verify journey has passed. We are making that proof repeatable rather than trusting a one-time success.
next: Build the staff-level permission wall so firm-wide meetings, actions, and Ask never show the wrong person's information.
Repair the four main entry points and keep the same client in view as the advisor moves between CRM, Meetings, and Ask.
Prove one deep replacement journey: start the day, open a client, run a meeting, approve the CRM and task changes, send the human-reviewed outcome, and ask a cited follow-up question.
decisions: Keep Lantern's current foundation. Restarting on an open-source CRM would throw away too much working, specialized value.
Reuse and repair existing Lantern systems before building new ones. Many missing-looking features are already partly or fully present.
Use open-source products as parts and proven patterns where they truly save time, not as a forced replacement for Lantern.
Study Wealthbox and Jump closely. Borrow their useful workflows and system ideas, then make Lantern's version simpler, more connected, and more trustworthy.
sections.holdTitle: What we are deliberately not doing yet
hold: We are not restarting the whole product from scratch.
We are not adding firm-wide views before staff permissions are safe.
We are not rebuilding engines that already exist just because the front end does not expose them clearly.
We are not calling the app ready until the same installer and core journey pass on real Windows computers.
sections.bottomText: Much of Lantern's foundation is already built, but the remaining work is the work that turns a large collection of features into a dependable product. The smartest move is to finish proof, connect what already exists, and build one excellent advisor journey that can honestly replace Wealthbox and Jump.

sections.title: Strategic Advisor Memo
sections.now: A hard-nosed, investor-grade read of the REAL Keepance (built from the code, the docs, fresh market research, and an independent Codex pass told to argue the opposite). It exists to answer one question: can this become a real company that creates meaningful wealth in five years? It is intentionally tough on the idea because the product is good enough to deserve a real test, not another build cycle. Every section below is the full memo, just made scannable; a longer source version and the action-plan companion are also saved in the Keepance project for the team.
sections.intro: Bottom line up front: an unusually good product chasing an unproven need. The advisor direction is the soundest of its five re-aims, but it rests on a single advisor's pain signal, and the privacy wedge is a trust-accelerator, not a must-buy. The only correct move is to narrow to one bulletproof job and let real, arm's-length advisors prove or disprove demand in 60 days.

blocks.title: One-sentence verdict
blocks.lead: Keepance is an unusually good product chasing an unproven need: narrow to ONE bulletproof job and run a hard 60-day demand test (10-15 advisor talks → 5 demos → 3 real-data pilots → 3-5 weekly users, 1-2 paying or signed letters of intent, zero speculative features). If it fails, do NOT re-pivot to a sixth target — park it or switch to a done-for-you services motion.
body: An independent Codex pass, told to argue the opposite, reached the SAME call: narrow, not kill and not build-harder. It sharpened three things — lead with the pain (privacy is the permission to try, not the reason to buy), say 'less to vet' not 'nothing to vet', and keep one sales-unlocking integration in scope even during the feature freeze.

blocks.title: First-principles gut-check — is this a real business?
blocks.lead: Real problem (mild) · real person (narrow) · real budget (already spent) · real promise (unproven) · real advantage (not in distribution) · real-but-modest scale. That clears the bar for a 60-day test. It does NOT clear the bar for another year of building.
bullets: 1) The real problem: 'walk into every meeting already knowing the whole household, without digging through scattered files and a search box that doesn't work.' The job is retrieval/recall, not drafting. The one real pain signal on record is exactly this. Honest caveat: it's an annoyance, not a bleeding wound — and 'annoying but survivable' is the hardest pain to sell against.

2) Who's affected: the small independent fee-only RIA (roughly 1-20 people) where client context is scattered and nobody owns it — NOT 'advisors' broadly, not wirehouses, not big firms. The 3-20 person firms may feel the pain MORE than solos. Lead with the pain; privacy is the permission to try.

3) What they pay now: a small RIA spends ~3.8-6% of revenue on tech (~$300-600 per advisor per month for CRM + planning + portfolio), plus $49-120/mo for a single AI notetaker. Real budget exists — but it's already fully allocated, and 'AI that knows my client' is starting to arrive bundled at $49/mo inside tools they already pay for.

4) The unique promise: 'one private, cited brief of everything you know about a household — built automatically from your own files, that never leaves your computer.' Synthesis + local. No competitor credibly says both today. Real sentence; not yet proven to be a BUYER's deciding sentence.

5) The unfair advantage: design taste + AI-leveraged build speed + a live in-household advisor (the wife, a CFP) + a hard-to-copy architecture. Honest limit: none of it is a DISTRIBUTION advantage, and distribution is the whole game.

6) Can it scale: base case is a cash-flow business (~95% margin; 150-350 customers ≈ $300K/yr; ~1,000 ≈ $1M/yr) — a great solo outcome. Venture-scale as a standalone app means a capital war it loses; the one real venture path is licensing the engine to a CRM/custodian. Plan for cash-flow; treat the rest as upside.

blocks.title: Reality check — what's real vs. what drifted
blocks.lead: The product engine is genuinely built; the story it tells about itself is not consistent across surfaces. That inconsistency is itself a trust problem for a trust product.
bullets: REAL (code-verified): the 3-tab app (Client Map · Ask · Workflows), the auto-built cited Client Map, cited Q&A over the client's own files (real local search + citation-checking), the in-house Word engine with tracked changes, local-first + bring-your-own-key, and the OneDrive + Wealthbox connectors.
NOT what the brief said: Box / ShareFile / Jotform / Zocks connectors do NOT exist in code (only one placeholder logo). The 'embedded local model' is still aspirational (external Ollama only today).

DRIFT (fix before any advisor sees it): the live site is reportedly advisor-framed now, but the pricing config still says 'attorney / litigator', the in-repo homepage still says 'law practice', and the features doc is two pivots stale. The pricing config reaches the in-app checkout, where the law copy AND a $99-vs-$948 price inconsistency are live.
Nothing advisor-polished has SHIPPED yet — the Client Map + advisor re-aim are finished in code but not packaged into an installer a customer can download.

blocks.title: The strongest version of the idea
blocks.lead: Not 'a private AI workspace for advisors.' It's: 'the thing that reads the pile of files you already have on a household and hands you back one cited brief you can trust in a meeting — and because it runs on your machine, your compliance officer has nothing to vet.'
body: One person, one job, one trust story. It wins by being the deepest at synthesis-across-documents (the least-crowded angle in the whole landscape) and the only one that is truly local. Demo-led, founder-sold, priced as a serious tool ($1,500-3,000/yr, not $99), and ruthlessly NOT a notetaker.

blocks.title: The weakest version (the one that fails)
blocks.lead: 'A privacy-first AI assistant for financial advisors.' It fails because 'AI assistant' is the most crowded sentence in the category, 'privacy-first' is now claimed by everyone and maps to no legal mandate, and it's a horizontal tool an advisor has to learn and change their workflow for.
body: That version is 'yet another login', and advisors drop those. Today's public surface is dangerously close to it — except worse, because parts of it still say 'law practice.'

blocks.title: Market diagnosis & ICP ranking
blocks.lead: The market is real but FLAT — a share-shift game, not a growth wave (~33,000 RIA firms; advisor headcount ~283,000, flat for a decade). You win by taking share. The one tailwind is AI adoption itself (advisor gen-AI use jumped 41%→52% in a year).

rows: Solo / small fee-only RIA (1-20p) where context is scattered
Buyer=user=compliance owner at the small end; no staff to mask the pain; local-first lands hardest; warm access exists
Most documents per household = most synthesis pain
Adjacent, doc-heavy, privacy-minded; but Holistiplan owns tax-doc reading
Real money & pain, but demand SOC 2 / DPA / entity Keepance lacks
Largest headcount, but the firm dictates the stack — can't buy
Never validated; legal AI is ~10x more capitalized (Harvey $11B)

body: The honest tension: the #1 wedge (privacy-caring + small + acutely feels synthesis pain) may be a small intersection. Sizing it is the single most important unknown the 60-day test must resolve.

blocks.title: Core customer pain — sorted honestly
blocks.lead: Sell the one urgent job; don't fight the solved ones.
bullets: Real & urgent: 'I can't quickly find what I know about this household before a meeting.' (The validated signal. The beachhead.)
Nice-to-have: auto-drafting the review note / Reg BI rationale. Useful, but ChatGPT already does the blank page; not a switch-driver alone.
Fake-but-sounds-good: 'advisors are desperate for privacy-first AI.' They're cautious about cloud AI (real); desperation is the founder's projection.
Already solved (don't fight): meeting notes (Jump/Zocks/Wealthbox), tax-return reading (Holistiplan), estate docs (Vanilla).
Won't-trust-AI-with-yet: anything that ACTS on client data autonomously. Keepance's 'AI proposes, human decides, everything cited' posture is correctly conservative.

blocks.title: Wedge recommendation
blocks.lead: The solo/small RIA's pre-meeting prep. Trigger: a review meeting on the calendar. Workaround today: re-reading the plan + scrolling the CRM + a broken email search. Why Keepance is 10x: it reads the household's OWN files and produces a cited brief — no migration, point it at the folder they already have.
body: The wedge IS the Client Map. Everything else (drafting, the Reg BI note, a shared firm brain) is a later expansion that only earns its place once one advisor can't live without the first job.

blocks.title: Product strategy — what to be FIRST
blocks.lead: Be the Client Map, on local data, bulletproof — and nothing else for 60 days. The hero loop is REAL today; the work is reliability and onboarding, not new capability.
bullets: Essential v1 (the one loop): point at a client folder → Client Map builds itself (cited, gaps flagged) → ask a pre-meeting question, click the source → draft one review note.

Freeze (impressive, near-zero willingness-to-pay today): the firm/team encrypted tier, live multi-user co-editing, single sign-on, the embedded local model, every connector beyond OneDrive + Wealthbox, and any new vertical.

Fix before any advisor sees it (credibility, not features): the pricing config's law copy + the $99-vs-$948 inconsistency; the stale in-repo homepage and features doc; the dev email still wired into the demo machine.

blocks.title: Trust & adoption barriers
blocks.lead: The trust gap is the firm-sale gate — but most of it is manageable if you sell solos first and stay scrupulously honest.

rows: Fatal for firms, manageable for solos (who are their own compliance owner). Form the LLC now; defer SOC 2 until a deal demands it.
The 'private' claim has a cloud asterisk
Manageable → selling point IF honest. True only in local mode; bring-your-own-key still sends the query to the AI provider (never to a Keepance server). Say 'less to vet,' not 'nothing to vet.'
Reg S-P vendor oversight (small-RIA deadline June 3, 2026)
Selling point: a genuine diligence-reducer for no-compliance-officer firms — but a convenience, not a legal mandate (the rule assumes vendors; the SEC's AI/cyber proposals were withdrawn).
Must-address: local must still log / retain / export AI work product, or it trades one gap for another.
Real: a fiduciary equates a certified vendor with safety. Counter with design polish + a case study + the entity.
Already handled well: cited answers + 'refuse rather than bluff.' Lead with it.

blocks.title: Positioning & messaging
blocks.lead: Own the category 'private client-intelligence' (not 'AI assistant', not 'notetaker', not 'document vault'). Lead 70% outcome, 30% privacy.
bullets: Homepage headline: 'Walk into every meeting already knowing the whole household.'

Subheadline: 'Keepance reads the files you already have and builds one cited brief of each client — on your own computer, so there's far less for compliance to vet (and in local mode, nothing leaves at all).'
10-sec pitch: 'It turns the pile of files on a client into one trustworthy, cited brief you can ask anything — and it all stays on your machine.'

Skeptical-advisor pitch: 'You already have the documents. You already pay for a CRM. This isn't another system to migrate into — it reads what you have, runs on your machine, and your compliance officer has nothing new to approve.'
Language to avoid: 'compliant', 'guaranteed', bare 'secure', 'revolutionary/seamless/transform', 'AI assistant', and anything implying it gives financial advice (SEC is fining AI-washing).

blocks.title: Competitive landscape — where it can win, and can't
blocks.lead: The commodity layer (notes) is being absorbed by CRMs at ~$50/mo. Keepance's only defensible lane is cross-document cited SYNTHESIS — the one brief that the per-document specialists, the CRMs, and generic ChatGPT all fail to deliver.
bullets: Do-nothing / ChatGPT-or-Copilot by hand (the REAL default): win on cited answers over their own files with no copy-paste + local privacy. Lose if their firm already standardized on Microsoft Copilot (enterprise data protection erodes the privacy argument).
Notetakers (Jump ~$105M / ~27k advisors; Zocks ~$65M): do NOT fight. Position as complementary; the notes race is over.

CRMs embedding AI (Wealthbox AI $49/mo, 25k advisors, $200M raised; Orion Denali; Salesforce): the most dangerous trend ('already in your stack'). Win only on depth + local; the Wealthbox connector is smart, competing with Wealthbox's AI is not.
Doc specialists (Holistiplan tax; Vanilla estate; FP Alpha; Powder): they own per-document-type; win on cross-document synthesis into one brief.

FutureVault (closest competitor): same 'documents → cited intelligence' promise, but cloud, enterprise-only, SOC 2, blue-chip logos. The answer Jameson must be able to say: 'FutureVault puts your clients' lives in their cloud; Keepance keeps them on your machine — and a solo can start this afternoon.'

blocks.title: Defensibility — graded honestly (2-3 / 5)
blocks.lead: Enough for a cash-flow niche business; not enough to hold off a funded land-grab if one targets the local-first wedge.
bullets: Trust/architecture moat (the real one, moderate): true local-first + in-house Word engine + the Client Map is genuinely hard for cloud incumbents to copy because it fights their business model. A moat of positioning, not patents.
Workflow lock-in (weak now, strong later): once a book's institutional memory lives in the Client Maps, switching cost is high. Doesn't exist until weekly use.
Data moat: none — by design the data stays the customer's and local. Privacy and data-network-effects are in tension; accept it.
Distribution moat: none. This is the gap that decides everything.
Founder insight (real): an in-household CFP + a designer who can ship.

blocks.title: Business model & pricing
blocks.lead: Fix the self-inflicted wound first: the pricing config says $468/$948/$1,548 with ATTORNEY copy while the advisor page floats $99/yr — a 10x inconsistency on a trust product. Then test HIGHER, not lower.
bullets: Recommended first-wedge pricing (test, don't assume): Solo ~$1,800/yr (~$150/mo); small-firm ~$1,200/seat/yr (3+ seats); a premium 'with-onboarding' pilot at $2,500-3,000. Advisors spend $3,600-7,200/yr on the core stack; $99 signals 'not for real practices.'
Model: per-seat ANNUAL (matches advisor budgeting + the ~95% bring-your-own-key margin); founder-led PAID pilots first; no self-serve funnel until the demo is reliable and a price is validated.
The margin truth: bring-your-own-key = customer pays inference = ~95% gross margin. Break-even is ~150 customers, not thousands.

blocks.title: Go-to-market (low-budget, founder-led)
blocks.lead: Founder-led hand-selling, not a funnel. The first paying customer must be a STRANGER, not the wife's firm.
bullets: First 20 conversations: arm's-length solo RIAs via XYPN forums, NAPFA, fee-only advisor groups, FinTwit — plus warm intros the design partner makes to PEERS at other firms. Use Mom-Test discovery (workflow questions, not demos).
Distribution kingmakers: Kitces (get on the AdvisorTech map), XYPN (apply to XYPN LIVE), T3, and custodian marketplaces (Altruist/Schwab/Fidelity) once there's a reference customer.

Services-first on-ramp (an angle the memo was underweighting): early buyers often want the OUTCOME done for them, not software. Offer a paid 'private client-intelligence setup' — clean their folders, connect their tools, build their first Client Maps — charge a setup fee PLUS subscription. The concierge work IS the validation, and can be the whole business if software-only stalls.
Local-Utah angle: the design partner's firm + the local advisor chapter for warm, in-person first demos.

blocks.title: Validation plan (before any more building)
blocks.lead: Test the demand, not the code. The funnel: 10-15 conversations → 5 demos → 3 real-data pilots → 3-5 weekly users → 1-2 paying or signed letters of intent. Measure your selling behavior as closely as the market's response.
bullets: H1 — is the pain acute enough to pay? 10 Mom-Test calls with arm's-length solos. Validating: they describe it unprompted + ask 'when can I have it.' Invalidating: polite interest, no urgency.
H2 — does the Client Map wow on THEIR messy files (not just the demo household)? Build a map live from a pilot's real folder.
H3 — is local-first a reason to BUY or just a comfort? A/B the pitch (outcome-led vs privacy-led).
H4 — will they pay ~$1,500+? Ask for a paid pilot ($500-1,500 / 90 days). A signed pilot from a stranger is the proof.
H5 — does weekly use stick? Track real logins over 4 weeks.
Concierge MVP: for one pilot, build their first 5 Client Maps by hand — prove value before trusting the automation.

blocks.title: Five-year wealth path
blocks.lead: Base case is a cash-flow business, not a venture rocket — but 'venture is impossible' is too strong: there's a narrow infrastructure-licensing path. Plan for cash-flow; treat the rest as upside.

rows: Becomes a consultancy, not a product
Venture: license the engine to a CRM/custodian
No reference traction = no partner wants it

blocks.title: Founder-specific strategy
blocks.lead: The unfair advantage is design taste + a working product + unusually close access to one real advisor workflow. The biggest weakness is the BUILD TRAP — and five re-aims is the tell.
bullets: The build trap: each pivot was a new BUILD, not a new set of customers. A designer's instinct under uncertainty is to make the thing better; the job now is to make someone buy it.

The warm-path risk: the wife is design partner #1 but her firm 'can't be first to buy' (her career depends on it). So the warmest asset is compromised as a validation source. Use her for workflow truth, vocabulary, sample data, and peer intros — not as proof. The first paying customer must be a stranger.
The fix: commit 50%+ of Keepance time to CUSTOMERS (discovery, demos, pilots); let the AI do the building. The one thing only Jameson can do is sell.

blocks.title: Brutal risks — the top of the list
blocks.lead: The two that matter most: the pain isn't acute enough to pay for, and the build trap recurs (a sixth pivot instead of selling). Both are High severity, High likelihood.

rows: Pain real but not acute enough to pay
Discovery calls = polite interest, no urgency
Build trap recurs (6th pivot, not selling)
A new positioning doc appears before 3 paying customers
Client Map underwhelms on real messy files
Maps thin/wrong outside the demo sample
A funded incumbent ships true local
Competitor announces on-prem / self-serve small-RIA tier
Demo, checkout price, and docs tell different stories
No distribution; never gets in front of advisors

blocks.title: Decision memo
blocks.lead: NARROW + TEST. Not kill (the product + the in-household signal are too good to walk away unproven). Not build-harder (no evidence justifies it). Narrow to the one loop, fix the surface, and let arm's-length advisors decide in 60 days.
bullets: Best first ICP: solo / small (1-20p) independent fee-only RIA on Windows where context is scattered.
Best first workflow: pre-meeting prep → the cited Client Map → ask-a-question → draft one review note.
Best first product shape: the existing desktop app, advisor-default, the one loop bulletproof, OneDrive + Wealthbox only.
Best pricing hypothesis: ~$1,800/yr solo (test the flinch); kill the $99 line.
If the test fails: do NOT re-pivot to a sixth ICP — park it, or convert to the services/concierge motion.

blocks.title: Concrete action plan
blocks.lead: Today and this week is cleanup + conversations, NOT building.
bullets: Today: write the one-sentence FutureVault answer; start the Utah LLC; draft the advisor homepage headline; disconnect the dev email from the demo machine.

This week: fix the pricing config copy + resolve $99-vs-$948 to ONE advisor price; replace the law homepage with advisor framing; book 10 Mom-Test discovery calls; one clean end-to-end demo rehearsal on a fresh Windows build.

Next 2 weeks: run the 10 calls; build one Client Map live from a real (sanitized) advisor folder; make the paid-pilot OR done-for-you ask to the 3 most-pained, landing ≥1 stranger; stand up one advisor landing page + demo-request capture.

Next 30 days: 2-3 paid real-data pilots used weekly; draft the design-partner case study; get on the Kitces map + apply to XYPN LIVE; verify the Wealthbox paste-key on the design partner's real paid account.
Next 90 days: 3-5 weekly-active + 1-2 paying/LOI, or park/services. Decide on real usage data, not feelings.

blocks.title: The 10 questions to answer before investing months more
blocks.lead: If you can't answer these with evidence, you're not ready to spend another quarter on it.
bullets: 1. Is the recall pain acute enough that an arm's-length advisor pays $1,500+ — or is it 'annoying but survivable'?
2. Does the Client Map actually wow on a real advisor's messy files, or only on the curated demo?
3. Is 'local-first' a reason a buyer CHOOSES you, or just a comfort they nod at while buying on outcome?
4. Can you get 5 arm's-length advisors in the room at all — i.e., do you have, or can you build, distribution?
5. Will a stranger pay before the wife's firm does?
6. Does the Wealthbox paste-key actually work on a paid account — does the 'fits your stack' story hold?
7. What's the real price — does $1,800/yr close, or only $99? What does that say about perceived value?
8. Are you willing to spend 50%+ of your time selling, not building — and to stop at the 6th-pivot temptation?
9. What's the honest 5-year goal — a $300K-1M/yr cash-flow business (likely) or a venture rocket (unlikely)?
10. If, in 60 days, 3-5 advisors are NOT using it weekly with 1-2 paying, will you actually stop — or rewrite the story again?

sections.title: Strategy & Vision
sections.now: Keepance competes head-on to be the LEADING financial-advisor AI — and it's a simple, powerful AI app, not a note-taker: connect your files → ask cited questions → get a living Client Map, all kept private on the advisor's own machine. Vision: every advisor walks into every meeting already knowing the whole household, without putting that family's data in someone else's cloud. We win on simplicity + AI-first clarity, not integration breadth (the incumbent Jump's failure mode is 'connect 60 things' — we won't become that). The beachhead is still solo and small independent / fee-only RIAs first, but the ambition is to win the category, not carve a defensive niche out of it. The private / local-first / Word-native / cited-Client-Map assets make the 'simple, powerful, AI-first, private' promise credible. Full detail in the linked Product Strategy report and the 2026-06-29 board decision.
decisions: BOARD DIRECTION (2026-06-29, OFFICIAL STANCE): Keepance competes head-on to be the LEADING financial-advisor AI — not a retreat to a niche — and positions as a simple, powerful AI app (connect your files → ask cited questions → living Client Map), NEVER a note-taker. Win on simplicity + AI-first clarity, not integration breadth (the incumbent Jump's failure mode is 'connect 60 things'). Notetaking is at most a feature, never the identity. This SUPERSEDES the 'reposition away from advisors / retreat to a narrow wedge' counsel in the 2026-06-28 competitive analysis + strategic advisor memo (kept as competitor/market intel, not direction). The 'get real first users, don't only build' discipline still holds.

PROOF SPRINT (2026-06-25): go all-in on first users for ~2 months — freeze big new features; land 3-5 advisors using Keepance weekly with 1-2 paying; make ONE aha-path bulletproof (pick client folder → build the Client Map → ask a cited question → draft a review note); and build the trust packet (entity + a data-flow sheet + scrub any 'compliant' wording).
RE-AIM (2026-06-24): pivot from law firms to financial advisors; the unit becomes a client / household, not a legal matter.
Beachhead locked: solo and small fee-only RIAs (own their stack, privacy-minded, buyer = user = compliance owner = short sales cycle).
Positioning: the private client-intelligence layer (a different category from cloud notetakers). Pitch 70% outcome, 30% privacy architecture.
Engineering decision: reuse the engine; do NOT rename internal matter/matter_id (the security isolation key); add a client/household label facade.
Sequencing: demo-first, then onboard real advisors, then build only what paying users ask for.
insights: Firsthand competitor read (2026-06-29): Jameson signed up for Jump (the incumbent, ~$105M funded, the most-adopted standalone advisor-AI tool) and went through the product and its AI videos directly. His assessment: Jump's AI is messy, scattered, and hard to use inside the actual product — it's 'connect 60 things, then send forms and take notes,' still a note-taking app at its core with a fuzzy AI direction. That is precisely the opening Keepance attacks by being simpler, clearer, and genuinely AI-first. This matches, independently, the competitive report's finding that Jump's synthesis is meeting/CRM-derived and its document capability is shallow.
The advisor re-aim is aiming at the demand that was actually observed: the strongest pain signal in the whole record came from a financial advisor, not a litigator. The law ICP was never validated.

This is ~70% designed-in already: an advisor mode, a shipped 7-template Advisor Practice Pack (Reg S-P / Reg BI), a financial-advisors site page, and a Client Map architected with 'household' as the advisor unit.
North Star metric set: weekly active advisors who ran a real client workflow. We steer by that, not signups.
The binding constraint is distribution + trust, NOT product features. The demo is the entry ticket; selling is the real work.

Two independent assessments on 2026-06-25 — our own research and an independent Codex review — reached the same verdict: an impressive pre-traction product whose binding constraint is distribution + trust. That agreement is why this direction is treated as settled, not another guess.

sections.title: Roadmap
sections.now: Themed, not dated, and reshaped by what real advisors ask for as we sell. The rule: build only what makes the CURRENT phase succeed. Right now that is the impressive demo; next is onboarding real advisors onto real data; later is whatever paying users actually demand. Nothing speculative. Full themes, metrics, and the prioritization gates are in the Product Strategy report.

lanes.label: NOW — the impressive, reliable demo
items: Advisor re-aim Phase 1: advisor language (client / household), a killer advisor sample household, advisor-neutral AI prompts, the Advisor Practice Pack featured, legal templates hidden.
The aha loop rock-solid end-to-end: open a client → it already knows the household → cited answer → drafted follow-up + a Reg BI / suitability note.
Verified on real Windows (a demo that crashes on stage is worse than no demo).
Done = you would proudly show it to any advisor and it will not break.

lanes.label: NEXT — onboard real advisors (first 5 paying)
items: Thin, read-only Wealthbox connector (seed Client Maps from the CRM's existing notes), then a OneDrive path (likely just point at the synced folder). Time-boxed; preserve local-first.
Trust artifacts: form the LLC, the CCO-forwardable security one-pager, the design-partner case study.
Founder-led onboarding that gets a new advisor to the aha fast.
Done = the design partner plus ~5 advisors paying and using it weekly.

lanes.label: LATER — shaped by paying users
items: More connectors (Redtail, custodians, planning tools like eMoney) — built per real demand only.
The firm / team tier for advisors (shared client context + information barriers) once trust artifacts justify it.
The deeper sensitivity model (replacing legal 'privilege') and richer household fields.
Meeting-notes capture only IF advisors repeatedly demand it (today: deliberately out; we complement Jump / Zocks, not compete).

sections.title: Marketing
sections.now: The marketing library is large and well-organized, but almost none of it drives traffic yet (~225 visitors over a recent ten-week stretch, nearly all direct). The re-aim points it at advisors: the website already has a strong /financial-advisors page and an advisor Reg S-P one-pager — those move to the front, the deeply-legal pages move off the main path, and the press-kit one-liner stops saying 'law practice.' Still a distribution problem at heart, not a copy problem.
decisions: Make the website advisor-first: lead with the financial-advisors page; demote legal pages; fix the press-kit 'private intelligence layer for a law practice' line.
Promote the assets that are already advisor-correct: the Reg S-P blog post, the advisor CCO one-pager, and the vs-Jump comparison.
All public copy stays bound to the voice guide (first-person, plain, no AI-cliché words, no em dashes, every claim linked).
insights: The Reg S-P angle is genuinely timely: the small-firm advisor compliance deadline just passed (June 2026), and local-first is a clean answer to vendor oversight.
The distribution kingmakers for advisor software are Kitces (Nerd's Eye View / the AdvisorTech map) and XYPN — getting on their radar is worth more than any ad.
Do not market hard until the advisor demo is genuinely reliable: shipping traffic to a shaky demo burns the first impression.

sections.title: Sales
sections.now: No paying customers yet. The plan is founder-led hand-selling, not self-serve signups or ads: win the design partner (Journey Beyond Wealth) first as the first real user, first customer, and source of warm referrals, then hand-sell the next 10-20 advisors with live demos on a controllable sample (not a prospect's live data on stage). A parallel go-to-market track (LLC, target list, pitch, outreach, CRM pipeline) runs now, while the demo is built.
decisions: Sell by hand, not by funnel: hand-sell the first ~10-20 advisors one at a time.
Journey Beyond Wealth = design partner → weekly real use → named testimonial + case study + referrals.
Win solo advisors first, not firms (the firm tier needs trust credentials Keepance lacks today).
Demo weighting ~70% outcome (knows the household, drafts the work, stays private), ~30% privacy architecture.
insights: The trust gate is the make-or-break: advisors' compliance officers will ask for a SOC 2 we don't have. Answer with the local-first / no-vendor-server story (client data never reaches a Keepance server, so most vendor-oversight burden does not apply) plus a CCO-forwardable one-pager.
Don't depend on one channel: beyond the design partner, build referrals + XYPN + NAPFA / FPA + advisor Facebook groups + a Kitces push.
Build and sell in parallel: do the LLC, target list, pitch, and outreach now so a warm pipeline is ready the moment the demo lands.
The demo path must be reliable before it's shown to an advisor.

The CCO-forwardable trust one-pager now has a first draft, fact-checked line-by-line against the actual app code. An independent review caught and fixed two over-claims before they could embarrass us, and the sheet honestly states what we do and don't have yet (no SOC 2 certificate, no signed data agreement).

sections.title: Growth & Traction
sections.now: Still the honest weak point: zero paying customers, near-zero inbound. The re-aim removes the single biggest blocker the law plan had: there is now a warm, real design partner and a validated pain signal in financial advice. But selling is still the work, and the product needs a genuine finishing pass alongside it. Idea-validation stage commercially, with a far better wedge than before.
decisions: Name reality plainly: a capable, mostly-built product meeting a market we are only now reaching warmly. Both finishing the demo and reaching buyers are real work.
Set an honest kill / scale signal: if hand-selling can't get ~3-5 advisors to pay AND use it weekly, the pain isn't acute enough; if it can, pour fuel on referrals + Kitces / XYPN.
Run building (the demo) and selling (the parallel GTM track) at the same time, every week.
insights: The math is encouraging: customers bring their own AI key (~95% gross margin), so a few hundred K needs only ~150-350 paying customers, well under 0.1% of the market.
Binding constraints, in order: (1) a reliable, impressive demo, (2) distribution / reach, (3) demo-to-close, (4) retention. Price is NOT the constraint.
Likely underpriced for advisors: they already spend $6-12K/yr on software vs. Keepance at ~$1K. Room to raise.
Structural risk to guard against: a product designer retreating into the codebase instead of selling (the 'build trap').

sections.title: Competitive & Market
sections.now: The advisor-AI space is hot and well-funded, but the leaders are a different category from Keepance. Jump (~$80M raised, claims ~1 in 10 US advisors), Zocks (~$45M), and Zeplyn are cloud, meeting-capture 'agentic operating systems' that sit above the CRM. Keepance is the private client-context + drafting layer that lives on the advisor's machine and complements those tools. We win the advisors who feel the cloud-privacy tension.
decisions: Do not fight the notetakers head-on. Position as the complementary private context + drafting layer; lead outcome + local-first (70/30).
Keep a competitor-watch log: the event that most threatens us is a funded notetaker shipping a genuinely local / no-vendor-server option.
Keep the advisor comparison pages (vs Jump / eMoney / ChatGPT) reconciled to current facts and honest about where rivals are the better choice.

Add FutureVault to the competitor watch as a 'document-vault / client-portal' rival (distinct from the notetakers). Re-check quarterly; the move that would most threaten us is FutureVault launching a self-serve small-RIA tier or a local/private deployment.
insights: FutureVault is our CLOSEST competitor: it makes almost the same pitch (a 'client life vault' with an AI insights engine shipped early 2026), but it is cloud-hosted and enterprise-only. That is exactly our wedge — client data on their servers vs. on the advisor's own machine, and slow big-firm sales vs. a solo who can start today.

Privacy is contested now (Zocks and Zeplyn both claim 'privacy-first'), so the defensible wedge is TRUE local-first (data physically never leaves the machine) + the depth of the Client Map + the clean Reg S-P vendor-oversight story.
Well-funded rivals prove the space is hot but don't attack the local-first wedge; they're meeting-notes-centric.
Advisors increasingly discover tools via search / ChatGPT and, above all, peer referrals; word-of-mouth is the highest-quality channel in wealth management.

sections.title: Engineering
sections.now: The engine is domain-generic and reused as-is: local-first file storage, the cited-recall RAG, the encrypted vault, the in-house Word (.docx) engine, live co-editing, SSO, and email import. The re-aim is a re-skin (advisor language, an advisor sample, advisor-neutral AI prompts, advisor templates), being built now by a parallel instance, demo-first. The product still needs finishing and hardening on real Windows. An independent Codex audit set the safe approach.
decisions: Reuse the engine; do NOT rename internal matter / matter_id or storage keys (the security isolation key) — use a user-facing client / household label facade.
Sequence: impressive demo first, THEN a thin Wealthbox connector, THEN OneDrive, THEN demand-driven connectors. Connectors are time-boxed and must preserve local-first.
Core-app rule unchanged: no shortcuts; build it robust and verified (TDD + Codex review). No autonomous build-cut or deploy without Jameson's explicit go.
insights: Codex independent audit (2026-06-24): the safe re-aim is a label facade, not a deep rename; renaming the isolation key would risk client-data-leak bugs across RAG / firm sync / saved data.
Real-Windows / Mac testing is the AI's job (Legion laptop), not Jameson's; the aha path reliability is part of 'demo done.'
The advisor product is ~70% there: advisor profession value, a 7-template advisor pack, and a Client Map designed for the household unit already exist.
Connectors to outside systems still carry vendor-access and scope risk — keep them thin, read-only, and behind the demo.

sections.title: UX
sections.now: The clean, navy-railed layout re-skins from the law identity (Matters / Search / Documents / Email / Workflows) to the advisor identity (Clients / Households). The centerpiece is the Client Map: the auto-built, cited 'everything I know about this household' profile that delivers the aha ('it already knows my client') in the first session. Trust stays a visible surface (where-your-data-is map, egress indicator, a forwardable confidentiality report). Onboarding to the aha fast is the retention make-or-break.
decisions: Client / household is the everyday unit label (via the facade), not 'matter.'
Keep trust visible and inspectable; keep the honest privacy-spectrum framing (local-only vs bring-your-own-key).
Optimize first-run hard for the first-session aha; founder-led onboarding for the first ~50 customers.
insights: Onboarding is do-or-die: ~75% of users churn in week one with poor onboarding, and the aha is 'the Client Map already knows my client' — remove every step before it.
The key UX change is the Client Map advisor rewrite (its prompts currently say 'legal assistant' and search for court terms).
Cited recall across files + email is the daily-use beachhead (meeting prep, annual-review prep, finding anything in the client's history).

sections.title: UI
sections.now: The two-layer design system (shared tokens + reusable components) and the polished light look (light background, dark text, navy accent, pink-to-blue gradient, Satoshi type) carry over unchanged. The only visual swaps for the re-aim are the photographic imagery (the hero currently shows an attorney with clients) and the example microcopy/screenshots that depict legal matters. Because Keepance sells trust, visual consistency is itself a trust signal.
decisions: Reuse the design system as-is; only swap attorney imagery and legal example microcopy for advisor equivalents.
Keep the light theme and the fixed per-screen layout law (header, one tools row, content).
Keep the Keepance shield identity; the logo and OG cards are vertical-neutral and need no change.
insights: The brand palette, type, logo, and social cards are vertical-neutral, so the UI re-aim is mostly imagery, not a restyle.
Real-hardware visual spot-checks (Word interop, native pickers, the auto-updater) still belong in the Testing pass.
A sloppy interface reads to a fiduciary as an unreliable vendor, so finishing the visual rough edges is part of earning trust.

sections.title: Testing
sections.now: Tracks how well Keepance actually works on each OS customers use. For the re-aim, the priority narrows: the advisor DEMO path (open client → Client Map → cited answer → draft) must be rock-solid on real Windows, because that is what every sales conversation rides on. Automated checks are strong on Linux (the build machine); real Windows is the priority to finish; Mac is largely untested. Real-OS testing is the AI's job, not Jameson's.

platforms.detail: The build/dev machine. Thousands of automated checks run here (unit, integration, browser, and a real-desktop harness). But Linux is not a customer platform, so green here does NOT mean green for real advisors.

The platform most advisors use, driven and tested by the AI on the always-on Legion laptop. For the re-aim, the bar is the advisor demo aha-loop running flawlessly on real Windows before it is shown to anyone. Hardening continues alongside.
Not yet validated on real Mac hardware (an M1 bench is available). Treat Mac as unverified until a real-hardware pass happens. Many advisors are on Windows, so Windows leads.

sections.title: Jameson's Questions
sections.now: Decisions and questions where Jameson (Board) makes the call. The five open ones below are the decisions the product strategy needs from him; the two at the bottom are earlier researched answers that still hold.

questions.q: Time split: will you commit at least half your week to customers (selling, design partner) vs. building?
questions.answer: Recommendation: yes, at least half, starting now. The build trap (a designer hiding in code) is the #1 risk; Claude/Codex build, your unique job is customers.

questions.q: Beachhead: are solo / small fee-only RIAs the right first target?
questions.answer: Recommendation: yes — they own their stack and the local-first story lands hardest. Override only if your warmest access is a different niche.

questions.q: Pricing: test a higher advisor price (or a new advisor tier) rather than inherit the lawyer pricing?
questions.answer: Recommendation: yes, test higher. Advisors spend $6-12K/yr on software; ~$1K is cheap, and too-low can read as not-serious.

questions.q: SOC 2 timing: defer it until a real deal demands it, leading with the local-first answer until then?
questions.answer: Recommendation: yes, defer. Form the LLC now; lead with no-vendor-server; pay for SOC 2 only when a customer says 'I'll sign once you have it.'

questions.q: North Star: steer by 'weekly active advisors who ran a real client workflow'?
questions.answer: Recommendation: yes. It captures real value delivered, not vanity signups. The full metric tree is in the Product Strategy report.

questions.q: Do our target users use Mac or Windows more?
questions.answer: Windows, by a wide margin, for the original (law) analysis (~81% Windows). Advisors are also predominantly Windows, though we lack advisor-specific first-party data yet. Takeaway unchanged: polish Windows first, support Mac as a strong second, keep Linux a low-priority long tail. Worth turning on OS tracking once traffic is real.

questions.q: What else could I be doing with AI to push this project forward?
questions.answer: The highest-leverage moves aren't 'write more code': (1) have AI drive/test the real Windows app like a user daily; (2) build one realistic advisor sample household as both the test yardstick and the demo; (3) run an AI lead-finding engine surfacing target advisors weekly with tailored outreach you approve. Plus an AI sales copilot. Skip social spam and big autonomous agents.

sections.title: Finance & Metrics
sections.now: No real revenue yet. Pricing carries over from 3.0 (per-seat annual: Solo $468 / Professional $948 / Firm $1,548 per seat, min 3) but is likely UNDERPRICED for advisors, who spend far more on software than the solo lawyers it was set for. The metric tree below is how we'll steer once customers exist. The one durable bright spot: customers bring their own AI key, so cost per customer is near zero (~95% gross margin).
decisions: Keep per-seat annual tiers, but TEST a higher advisor price (or a dedicated advisor tier) with the first cohort rather than inheriting lawyer pricing.
Keep the 'your files are always yours' guarantee: cancelling turns off AI features and updates, never your data.
Treat acquisition cost as founder-hours, not cash (spend is ~$0).
insights: North Star metric: weekly active advisors who ran a real client workflow. Metric tree underneath: conversations → demos → trials → activation (Client Map built on real data, target >60%) → weekly engagement → trial-to-paid → annual renewal → referrals.
The income math: at ~$948/yr that's ~315 customers for $300K; at the firm price, fewer. Roughly 150-350 paying customers / seats for the goal, well under 0.1% of the market.
SOC 2 / DPA / a formed entity are the firm-tier trust moat; defer SOC 2 until a deal needs it, but form the LLC now.
Re-run the model with real numbers only after the first ~10 advisors; until then, don't steer by it.

sections.title: Demo
sections.now: The advisor demo in four beats: onboard as an advisor, import a client's real files, watch the Client Map build itself, then ask the file anything and get cited answers. Runs in about 8 to 10 minutes, and everything stays on the machine.
sections.intro: What it proves: Keepance turns a pile of a client's files into a living, cited Client Map you can ask anything, all on your own computer, with no client data sent to an AI vendor.

steps.title: Onboard as an advisor
steps.do: Open Keepance for the first time. Choose Financial advisor when it asks what you do. Pick a local folder for your work, and add your AI key or choose a local model.
steps.say: This is your private workspace. It runs on your machine. You bring your own AI, or run it fully offline. Keepance itself never sees your clients' data.
steps.proves: It is advisor-native and private from the very first screen. There is no vendor in the middle.

steps.title: Import a client's files
steps.do: Create the household (use the Hendricks sample). Point Keepance at their folder: the financial plan, account statements, meeting notes, an email thread, and the beneficiary and estate notes. It imports and indexes them locally.
steps.say: Drop in everything you already have on this household. It stays in your own folders, on your own computer. Nothing is uploaded anywhere.
steps.proves: Real, scattered client material goes in, and none of it leaves the machine.

steps.title: The Client Map builds itself
steps.do: Open the Client Map. Watch it assemble from those files: household and key people, goals and priorities, accounts and holdings, risk and suitability, and a timeline of next actions. It flags gaps, like a risk profile that is over a year old, and cites where each fact came from.
steps.say: You did not fill any of this in. Keepance read the files and built the picture, and it tells you what is missing.
steps.proves: The map is generated from the client's real materials, with citations and gaps surfaced. This is the heart of the product.

steps.title: Ask the file anything
steps.do: In search, ask a real pre-meeting question: what did we decide about the Roth conversion, and where is that in writing? Read the short answer, then click the citation to open the exact file. Then ask: what is still open before their review?
steps.say: Now you can walk into any meeting and ask the file anything. Every answer points back to the source, so you can trust it and show your work.
steps.proves: Private, cited AI across the whole client. This is the private ChatGPT that actually knows your clients.

tips: Have the Hendricks sample household loaded and an AI key set before you start, so beat 2 onward is instant.
Building the Client Map live takes a moment. Narrate the privacy story (files stay local, you chose the AI) while it works.
Point at the egress indicator in the top bar: it shows exactly where each AI request went, or that nothing left the machine.
End on the cited answer in beat 4. It is the strongest moment: trustworthy AI that knows this specific client.
